newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - ScotPower pumps profits, eyes growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - ScotPower pumps profits, eyes growth.

text.p: British multi-utility Scottish Power Plc turned in a 38 percent jump in annual profits on Thursday, helped by contributions from its acquisitions, and promised further savings and organic growth.
"We are looking now to build our business organically, we're looking for growth in both the energy markets and the multi-utility markets," chief executive Ian Robinson said.

Scottish Power said pretax profits in the year ending March 31 jumped to 558.4 million pounds ($917.3 million) from 404.8 million pounds previously, largely as expected, and paid out a dividend of 18.50 pence, compared with 15.5 pence.
"They are delivering what they promised. They have their eye on the ball and are very focused on driving out the costs," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
Shares were up 2.5 pence to 396.5 pence by 0930 GMT after touching a high of 400 pence.

Scottish Power bought north west England regional electricity company Manweb in 1995, the first and only British generator to be allowed to make such a move, and added Southern Water to its stable last year after a tough battle with rival predator Southern Electric.
It set its 18.5 pence dividend target when it bought Southern and said it hoped to improve profitability by 52 million pounds and make disposals to bring in 100 million pounds.

Robinson said the company was ahead of schedule on these targets and that it expected cost savings to be around 25 million pounds by the end of the current financial year while disposals should be completed in the next 12 months.
At Manweb, Robinson said the cost base had come down to 60 million pounds in two years and that the company should be able to reduce costs further through joint operation of distribution.
Analysts had been looking out for signs that the company was benefiting from its acquisition strategy, achieving cost cuts and integration benefits.
"The key issue now is cost cutting, that is what we will be watching," the analyst said.
The purchase of Southern Water also helped Scottish Power to pay out the 19 percent rise in the dividend, Robinson said.
"The dividend is actually on what we see in the business and the quality of the business that we found at Southern Water," he said.

Finance director Ian Russell said the company felt that real dividend growth at its target of seven to eight percent was sustainable "for the next three years, say to the year 2000...we very much believe the performance of the business will support that."
